Thanks again for the call today, Alex - helpful to walk through your expected workload. Per our discussion, I wanted to capture the key SLO items and next steps so we have a shared checklist:

- P95 end-to-end latency target: 150ms or better for single-turn text generation (streaming acceptable)
- Baseline steady-state throughput: 200 reqs/s
- Peak/burst: 2.5x baseline for short windows (1-3 minutes)
- Typical concurrency per customer: 40-60 concurrent sessions
- Streaming: required for partial-token updates to the UI (client expects <60ms partial latency)
- SLA ask: 99.9% availability, with latency SLOs for p95

Thanks, Marissa - that captures it pretty well. A couple clarifications from our engineering team (Priya copied):

- The 150ms p95 is for single-turn generation returned as a streaming response to the client. For non-streaming responses p95 can be up to 250ms.
- Baseline 200 reqs/s is across our EU + US regions; US will see ~70% of traffic.
- Bursts are usually traffic surges when market data releases; we need the system to absorb 2.5x for up to 3 minutes without rejecting requests. Falling back to queued requests is OK as long as user shows progressive tokens immediately.
- Concurrency: 50 active sessions typical but occasionally 120 during spikes - we need graceful degradation under extreme spikes.

Also attached is a short doc with our sample traffic curve for a release day. Can you confirm typical scale-up times from idle (no warm GPUs) to being able to hit 200 reqs/s? And what options do you have for warm pools / pre-warmed capacity?

Great questions - below is a concise summary of how Redwood approaches these patterns and a recommended configuration for your SLOs. TL;DR: We can meet the p95 streaming targets with a mix of a small warm pool + fast scale-up and graceful queuing for extreme spikes.

Key behaviors and recommendations:

1) Warm pool options
- Warm VM/GPU pool: keep N GPUs idle with model loaded and KV cache warmed depending on model size. This gives near-immediate throughput and best p95. Typical recommendation for your profile: warm pool sized to handle ~30-40% of baseline (i.e., ~60-80 reqs/s).
- Pre-warmed containers: cheaper than full GPUs for fast cold-start of workers; useful as second-tier warm capacity.

2) Scale-up times
- From no warm GPUs to first GPU available: 30-90s depending on instance image (we optimize AMIs and container images for fast start).
- From first GPU to steady throughput to handle baseline: additional 30-120s as more instances come online and batching stabilizes.
- Note: streaming latency for the first partial tokens can still be kept low by routing to warm pool or pre-warmed containers.

3) Queueing and graceful degradation
- When capacity is constrained we offer prioritized queueing (by customer/session) and progressive streaming: clients see partial tokens immediately while remaining tokens are generated as capacity becomes available.
- Policies can drop or throttle non-critical traffic while protecting high-priority sessions.

4) Autoscaling/burst patterns
- Short bursts (<=3 minutes): recommended approach is warm pool sized for 30-40% baseline + short-term burst capacity that can scale to 2.5x baseline within ~120s.
- For release-day spikes, we can provision reserved burst capacity for the event window (temporary dedicated capacity) to guarantee headroom.

5) Observability & SLO monitoring
- We provide p50/p95/p99 latency dashboards, queue depth, warm-pool utilization, and per-route throttling counts. We can set alerts when p95 approaches threshold so we can engage runbook.

Attachments: Redwood-autoscale-patterns.pdf (examples) and Redwood-SLO-worksheet.xlsx (to capture your traffic profile).

- Optional: we can put together a short bench/POC with a 2-hour test run to validate streaming p95 in your environment.
